claims.text: The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is homogeneous, coarse-grained, and a single-phase solid solution.
Strain rate and temperature can be systematically varied in tensile or wear tests under inert or ultra-high-vacuum conditions.
Dynamic deformation of Co-free FeNiCrMn induces a strain-rate- and temperature-dependent near-surface transformation.
The near-surface transformation converts the original coarse-grained structure into an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer.
The ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer produces inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Inverse Hall-Petch behavior balances strength and ductility under specific loading conditions.
A regime exists in which deformation-induced microstructural changes occur without thermal diffusion dominating.
The transformation initiates locally at lattice defects and internal boundaries.
The localized transformation reduces the effective grain size.
Sufficient grain refinement places the alloy in an inverse Hall-Petch regime.
The proposed inverse Hall-Petch regime enhances strength without compromising ductility.
At intermediate to high strain rates, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have higher yield strength than the coarse-grained low-rate state or CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
At intermediate to high strain rates, Co-free FeNiCrMn will retain comparable or enhanced ductility relative to the baseline.
The strength-ductility effect will be greatest under conditions favoring formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer.
The proposed mechanism is applicable under inert or ultra-high-vacuum conditions.
Oxidation can dominate or alter the relevant near-surface microstructural evolution outside inert or ultra-high-vacuum conditions.
Excessive thermal diffusion can make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Processing variations may change the onset and extent of the dynamic transformation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes inverse Hall-Petch behavior caused by further grain-size reduction while also claiming that this refinement enhances strength. In the inverse Hall-Petch regime, further grain refinement conventionally reduces rather than increases strength; no intermediate optimum or alternative strengthening step is specified to reconcile these statements.
